```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(MASS)
library(nnet)

# MASS::select masks dplyr's, and we want dplyr's everywhere below
select <- dplyr::select

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")

# CASA palette, stated explicitly so the deck does not depend on casaviz
casa_purple <- "#4E3C56"
casa_teal   <- "#2E6260"
casa_yellow <- "#F9DD73"
casa_pink   <- "#E16FCA"
casa_green  <- "#9DBB65"
casa_red    <- "#C94C4C"
casa_cols   <- c("#2E6260", "#658E62", "#9DBB65", "#E7D870",
                 "#F3C486", "#E993AC", "#8F5289", "#4E3C56")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))

base_path <- here("sessions", "L6_data", "Performancetables_130242", "2022-2023")

# The DfE publishes suppressed / not-applicable values as codes, not blanks
na_all <- c("", "NA", "SUPP", "NP", "NE", "SP", "SN", "LOWCOV", "NEW", "SUPPMAT")

# Every file is keyed on URN. The LA and national summary rows carry no URN,
# and because dplyr joins NA to NA they would duplicate rows as well as not
# being schools - so they go before anything else happens.
read_dfe <- function(f) {
  suppressWarnings(
    read_csv(file.path(base_path, f), na = na_all, show_col_types = FALSE)
  ) |>
    mutate(URN = as.character(URN)) |>
    filter(!is.na(URN))
}

ks4 <- read_dfe("england_ks4final.csv") |>
  select(URN, ATT8SCR, P8MEA, TPUP, PTFSM6CLA1A, PTPRIORHI) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

absence <- read_dfe("england_abs.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

school_info <- read_dfe("england_school_information.csv") |>
  select(URN, SCHNAME, LANAME, MINORGROUP, OFSTEDRATING, OFSTEDLASTINSP)

destinations <- read_dfe("england_ks4-pupdest.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, COHORT, OVERALL_DEST) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

# Mainstream secondaries with an Ofsted judgement. Ofsted's five published
# grades collapse to four analytical ones: "serious weaknesses" and "special
# measures" are both categories of inadequate in Ofsted's own scheme, and
# separately they are far too small to model.
schools <- ks4 |>
  inner_join(absence, by = "URN") |>
  inner_join(school_info, by = "URN") |>
  filter(MINORGROUP %in% c("Academy", "Maintained school"),
         OFSTEDRATING %in% c("Outstanding", "Good", "Requires improvement",
                             "Serious Weaknesses", "Special Measures")) |>
  mutate(
    rating4 = case_when(
      OFSTEDRATING == "Outstanding"           ~ "Outstanding",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Good"                  ~ "Good",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Requires improvement"  ~ "Requires improvement",
      TRUE                                    ~ "Inadequate"),
    rating4 = factor(rating4,
                     levels = c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement",
                                "Good", "Outstanding"),
                     ordered = TRUE),
    below_good  = as.integer(rating4 %in% c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement")),
    outstanding = as.integer(rating4 == "Outstanding"),
    insp_year   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(substr(OFSTEDLASTINSP, 7, 10)))
  )

model_data <- schools |>
  drop_na(P8MEA, PTFSM6CLA1A, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10, TPUP, PTPRIORHI)

# One split, used by every classification model in the deck
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# AUC by the rank identity, so the deck needs no extra package
auc_of <- function(scores, actual) {
  r  <- rank(scores)
  n1 <- sum(actual == 1); n0 <- sum(actual == 0)
  (sum(r[actual == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

predictors <- ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
                log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP
```

## Recap {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Over three weeks we built a regression model up from a single scatter plot to a linear mixed effects model with random intercepts and random slopes
-   We learned a **recipe** - understand your data, start simple, add complexity only when it earns its place, and check your assumptions at every step
-   Last week we relaxed one particular assumption: that our observations were **independent**. Schools sit inside local authorities, and that grouping matters

## But one thing never changed {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Every single model we have fitted has had a **continuous outcome variable**
-   Attainment 8. Progress 8. Numbers that can take any value, that are roughly bell-shaped, and that happily sit on either side of a straight line
-   This choice let us use Ordinary Least Squares throughout - but we know that our data don't always look like this
-   What happens when the thing you want to explain is a *yes/no*, a *category*, or a *count*?

## This week's session aims {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Understand why OLS fails when the outcome is not continuous, and see it fail
-   Meet the **Generalised Linear Model (GLM)** - one framework, three moving parts
-   **Logistic regression** for binary outcomes, then ordinal and multinomial versions for categories
-   **Poisson regression** for counts, offsets for rates, and what to do about overdispersion
-   Throughout: can we predict a school's Ofsted rating from everything else we know about it?

# Back to Week 1 {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Remember these? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

In week 1 we spent a long time on **types of data**, and on the **distributions** that go with them.

| Data type | Example from our data | Distribution |
|---|---|---|
| Real-valued | Attainment 8 | Normal |
| Binary | Is this school single-sex? | Bernoulli / Binomial |
| Count | How many pupils on free school meals? | Poisson |
| Count, overdispersed | ... when the variance exceeds the mean | Negative binomial |
| Ordinal | Ofsted rating | *(no single answer)* |

. . .

We then spent three weeks modelling **only the first row**!

## The whole idea of a GLM, in one table {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| If your outcome is... | ...its distribution is | ...the model is |
|---|---|---|
| A continuous number | Normal | **OLS** - weeks 5, 6, 7 |
| A yes/no | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| A proportion out of a known total | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| An ordered category | - | **Ordinal logistic** |
| An unordered category | - | **Multinomial logistic** |
| A count | Poisson | **Poisson regression** |
| A count that is too variable | Negative binomial | **Negative binomial regression** |

. . .

**This is not seven new methods.** It is one method, with a slot you fill differently depending on what you are trying to explain.

## What actually changes {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Every GLM has exactly three pieces. You already know the middle one.

::: incremental
1.  **The random component** - what distribution does the outcome follow? (Normal, binomial, Poisson...)
2.  **The linear predictor** - $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + ...$ . This is *identical* to everything we have done for three weeks
3.  **The link function** - the bit of maths that connects the two, so that a straight line on one scale becomes a sensible prediction on the other
:::

. . .

OLS is just the GLM where the distribution is Normal and the link function does nothing at all.

## What a link function actually does {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The right-hand side of any regression is a straight line, and a straight line will cheerfully produce **any number at all**. The thing we are trying to predict usually cannot.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| Outcome | Its natural range | Link stretches it with | To get back, apply |
|---|---|---|---|
| A continuous number | $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ | *nothing needed* | *nothing* |
| A probability | 0 to 1 | $\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)$ | the logistic curve |
| A count | 0 to $+\infty$ | $\log$ | $\exp$ |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**The link is a translator.** It stretches a squashed scale out onto the whole number line, so the straight line has somewhere sensible to live. The top row needs no stretching - which is exactly why OLS is a GLM with the boring link.
:::

## Careful - this is not the same as logging your data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Back in **Vol 1** we fixed a curved relationship by taking logs of Attainment 8 and of % disadvantaged, then fitting OLS to the transformed values.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Transforming the data**

$$\log(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \epsilon_i$$

-   We change **every observation**
-   Then fit an ordinary model to the new numbers
-   Errors are assumed Normal *on the logged scale*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A GLM**

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i$$

-   The data are left **completely alone**
-   The link is applied to the **expected value**
-   The distribution does the work the transformation used to
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Which matters, because you *cannot* transform a binary outcome. A school is rated below Good or it is not - and $\log\left(\frac{0}{1-0}\right)$ is undefined. There is nothing to take the log of.

**The GLM never asks you to.** It models the probability behind the 0s and 1s, and leaves your data exactly as you found them.
:::

# Can we predict School Ofsted ratings? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Our question for today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   We have used Ofsted ratings as a **predictor** and as a **grouping variable** already
-   Today we turn it around and make it the **outcome**
-   *Given everything else we know about a school - its results, its intake, its absence rates, its size - can we predict what Ofsted said about it?*
-   And if we can, what does that tell us about what Ofsted is actually measuring?

-   **Note**, *Ofsted has changed how it rates schools now, so single-word ratings are no longer given*

## The outcome variable {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 95%

model_data |>
  count(rating4) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating4, y = n, fill = rating4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_red, casa_pink, casa_teal, casa_green)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Schools",
       title = "Ofsted ratings, mainstream secondaries in England") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
`r comma(nrow(model_data))` schools with complete data. Note immediately how **lopsided** this is - we will come back to that, because it causes more trouble than anything else today.
:::

## First attempt: just use OLS? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-  Let's re-code our ratings: "below Good" as **1** and "Good or better" as **0**
-  We can regress it on Progress 8 exactly as we have been doing for the last three weeks.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lpm <- lm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data)
summary(lpm)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lpm_range <- range(fitted(lpm))
lpm_neg   <- sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)
# What the straight line predicts for a solidly above-average school, used in
# the caption on the next slide. Computed rather than typed so it cannot drift
# if the filters on model_data ever change.
p8_one    <- as.numeric(predict(lpm, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = 1)))
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The model runs. It produces coefficients. It produces an R². Nothing errors.

**And its fitted values run from `r round(lpm_range[1], 3)` to `r round(lpm_range[2], 3)`.**
:::

## A probability of minus fifty percent? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 95%

grid <- tibble(P8MEA = seq(min(model_data$P8MEA), max(model_data$P8MEA), length.out = 300))
grid$lpm <- predict(lpm, newdata = grid)
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
grid$glm <- predict(glm1, newdata = grid, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 1, ymax = Inf,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_jitter(data = model_data, aes(P8MEA, below_good),
              height = 0.03, alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, lpm, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, glm, colour = "Logistic curve"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Mark the single point the caption talks about, so it can be found on the
  # graph rather than taken on trust
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = p8_one, colour = casa_red, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 1.45, y = p8_one, yend = p8_one - 0.18,
           colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = p8_one - 0.21, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           colour = casa_red,
           label = sprintf("Progress 8 = +1\npredicts %.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Logistic curve" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  # The caption talks in percentages, so the axis does too - a probability
  # axis labelled 0.00-1.00 against a caption saying "-13%" invites exactly
  # the question of where the -13% is supposed to be
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Progress 8 score", y = "P(rated below Good)",
       title = "The shaded bands are impossible probabilities") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
-  The straight line gives **`r comma(lpm_neg)` schools a negative probability** of being rated below good. 
-  At a Progress 8 of +1 it predicts a probability of being rated below good of about **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)`** (impossible). 
-  The logistic curve cannot do this - it is bounded at 0 and 1 by construction.
:::

## Where the curve comes from {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We need something that takes a straight line, which runs from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, and squashes it into $[0,1]$.

::: incremental
-   Start with the **probability** $p$ - bounded at 0 and 1, e.g. 0.4 (40%), awkward
-   Turn it into **odds**, $\frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{probability of happening}{probability of NOT happening}$ or $\frac{0.4}{0.6} = 0.67$ - now bounded at 0 and $+\infty$, better
-   Take the **log** of that ($\log\left(\frac{0.4}{0.6}\right) = -0.40$) - now unbounded in both directions :tada:
:::

. . .

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

-   That left-hand side is the **logit**, and it ***is*** the link function. The right-hand side is exactly the model we have been fitting since week 5.
-   A **logit** simply is a mathematical function that converts a probability (between 0 and 1) into a log-odds value that can range from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$
-   The link-function converts the expected value of the outcome (the mean) into something a straight line can cope with


## Odds are not probabilities {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Worth pausing, because this trips people (including me!) up all the time.

| Probability | Odds | In words |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 1.0 | Evens |
| 0.75 | 3.0 | Three to one on |
| 0.9 | 9.0 | Nine to one on |
| 0.1 | 0.11 | Nine to one against |

. . .

Probabilities are bounded above. **Odds are not.** That is the whole reason we work with them.

## And odds are not odds *ratios* {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Odds** describe **one** situation

$$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}$$

*"This school's odds of being rated below Good are 0.10"*
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
**An odds ratio** compares **two**

$$\text{OR} = \frac{\text{odds}_A}{\text{odds}_B}$$

*"...which is 0.07 times the odds of a school one Progress 8 point worse"*
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   Easily the most common mistake in reading logistic output. 
-   The odds are the raw ingredient; 
-   the **ratio** is what you get when you put two of them side by side -   and the **odds-ratio** is what a regression coefficient hands you.
:::

## Why the coefficient *is* a ratio {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Our model says the log-odds are a straight line:

$$\log(\text{odds}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

::: incremental
-   At $x$, the log-odds are $\beta_0 + \beta_1x$
-   At $x+1$, they are $\beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_1$
-   So the **difference in log-odds is just** $\beta_1$
-   And subtracting logs is the same as dividing...
:::

. . .

$$e^{\beta_1} = \frac{\text{odds at } x+1}{\text{odds at } x}$$

**A ratio of two odds** - because the coefficient was a difference of two log-odds all along.

## See it in our own data {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Single-predictor model, so the arithmetic is visible. glm1 is already fitted
# on the "minus fifty percent" slide.
odds_at <- function(x) {
  p <- predict(glm1, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = x), type = "response")
  as.numeric(p / (1 - p))
}
b1 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)["P8MEA"])

tibble(
  `Progress 8`  = c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
  Probability   = sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2),
                    ~ as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA = .x), type = "response")))),
  Odds          = sprintf("%.4f", map_dbl(c(-1, 0, 1, 2), odds_at)),
  `Odds ÷ the row above` = c("-", sprintf("%.3f", map_dbl(c(0, 1, 2),
                    ~ odds_at(.x) / odds_at(.x - 1))))
) |> kable(align = "rrrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The coefficient on Progress 8 is **`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`**, and $e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)`}$ = **`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(b1))`**.

That is the last column, every time. **One coefficient, one odds ratio, valid wherever you start from.** Now look at the probabilities - they fall `r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=-1), type="response")))` → `r sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=0), type="response")))` → `r sprintf("%.3f", as.numeric(predict(glm1, data.frame(P8MEA=1), type="response")))`, doing nothing so tidy. Which is exactly why *"the probability falls by X"* is never a safe reading of a logistic coefficient.
:::

# Binary logistic regression {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Running the model {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Same formula interface you have used for three weeks. Two differences: `glm()` not `lm()`, and a `family` argument.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_below <- glm(update(predictors, below_good ~ .),
                   data   = train,
                   family = binomial)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
ct <- summary(logit_below)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term        = rownames(ct),
  Coefficient = round(ct[, 1], 3),
  `Std. error`= round(ct[, 2], 3),
  `p`         = ifelse(ct[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(ct[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

## These coefficients are on the log-odds scale {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   A coefficient of `r round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2)` on Progress 8 does **not** mean "the probability falls by `r abs(round(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"], 2))`"
-   It means the **log-odds** fall by that much, for every one-point increase in Progress 8
-   Nobody thinks in log-odds. So we exponentiate, and get an **odds ratio**

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
**One extra Progress 8 point multiplies the odds of being rated below Good by about `r round(exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"]), 2)`** - that is, it cuts them by roughly `r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(logit_below)["P8MEA"])))`%.
:::

## Reading odds ratios {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 92%

or_tbl <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(logit_below)),
  est  = coef(logit_below),
  se   = summary(logit_below)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(or = exp(est), lo = exp(est - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(est + 1.96 * se),
         term = recode(term,
           "P8MEA" = "Progress 8",
           "PTFSM6CLA1A" = "% disadvantaged",
           "PERCTOT" = "% overall absence",
           "PPERSABS10" = "% persistently absent",
           "log(TPUP)" = "log(cohort size)",
           "PTPRIORHI" = "% high prior attainers",
           "MINORGROUPMaintained school" = "Maintained (vs academy)"))

ggplot(or_tbl, aes(x = or, y = fct_reorder(term, or))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, colour = casa_purple) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = casa_teal) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Odds of being rated below Good",
       subtitle = "Left of the dashed line = protective; right = raises the odds")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Anything whose interval crosses **1** is doing nothing detectable. Note how much work Progress 8 is doing compared with everything else.
:::

## So how good is it? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
p_below <- predict(logit_below, newdata = test, type = "response")
accuracy <- mean((p_below > 0.5) == test$below_good)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
baseline <- max(mean(test$below_good), 1 - mean(test$below_good))
auc_below <- auc_of(p_below, test$below_good)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
**Test-set accuracy: `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * accuracy)`**
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em"}
Not bad! Nearly nine schools in ten classified correctly.
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #C94C4C"}
**Now watch.**
:::

## The single most important slide today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 90%

tibble(
  model = c("Our logistic model", "A model that always\nsays 'not below Good'"),
  acc   = c(accuracy, baseline)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(model), y = 100 * acc, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc)), hjust = -0.15, size = 6) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_teal, casa_red)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Test-set accuracy (%)",
       title = "Our model versus a model that does nothing at all") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A model that makes **the same prediction every single time**, with no data at all, scores `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)`. Our model beats it by **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (accuracy - baseline))` percentage points**.
:::

## Why accuracy lied to us {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cm <- table(Actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better"),
            Predicted = ifelse(p_below > 0.5, "Below Good", "Good or better"))
kable(cm)
```

::: incremental
-   Only **`r comma(sum(test$below_good))`** of the `r comma(nrow(test))` test schools are actually below Good - the class is **rare**
-   The model catches **`r cm["Below Good", "Below Good"]`** of them and misses **`r cm["Below Good", "Good or better"]`**
-   If you were Ofsted, trying to decide which schools to visit, this model would be close to useless *at this threshold*
:::

. . .

**Always, always compare your accuracy against the majority-class baseline.** On imbalanced data, accuracy on its own is not evidence of anything.

## But the model is not useless {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Accuracy asks "did you get it right?" at one arbitrary cut-off. A better question is "**do you rank schools sensibly?**"

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

thr <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 300)
roc <- map_dfr(thr, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

p_roc <- ggplot(roc, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate",
       title = sprintf("ROC curve - AUC = %.3f", auc_below))

p_box <- tibble(p = p_below,
                actual = ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = actual, y = p, fill = actual)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_pink, casa_teal)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted probability",
       title = "Predictions, by what actually happened") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_roc + p_box
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**AUC = `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_below)`** - pick a below-Good school and a Good-or-better school at random, and the model gives the below-Good one a higher score `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auc_below)` of the time. That is genuinely useful. The problem was never the model - it was the **0.5 threshold**, which is a choice, not a law.
:::

## Moving the threshold {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

sweep <- map_dfr(seq(0.02, 0.9, by = 0.01), function(t) {
  pred <- p_below > t
  tibble(threshold = t,
         `Caught (recall)`   = mean(pred[test$below_good == 1]),
         `Correct when flagged (precision)` =
            ifelse(sum(pred) == 0, NA, mean(test$below_good[pred] == 1)))
}) |>
  pivot_longer(-threshold)

ggplot(sweep, aes(threshold, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(casa_purple, casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Classification threshold", y = NULL,
       title = "There is no free lunch here") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Drop the threshold and you catch more struggling schools, but more of your flags are false alarms. **Which error is worse is a policy question, not a statistical one** - and that is the right way round.
:::

## A second outcome, same story {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_out <- glm(update(predictors, outstanding ~ .), data = train, family = binomial)
p_out <- predict(logit_out, newdata = test, type = "response")
acc_out <- mean((p_out > 0.5) == test$outstanding)
base_out <- max(mean(test$outstanding), 1 - mean(test$outstanding))
auc_out <- auc_of(p_out, test$outstanding)

tibble(
  Model = c("Below Good vs Good+", "Outstanding vs rest"),
  Accuracy = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(accuracy, acc_out)),
  Baseline = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(baseline, base_out)),
  AUC = sprintf("%.3f", c(auc_below, auc_out)),
  `Caught at p > 0.5` = c(
    sprintf("%d of %d", cm["Below Good", "Below Good"], sum(test$below_good)),
    sprintf("%d of %d", sum(p_out > 0.5 & test$outstanding == 1), sum(test$outstanding)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

-   Higher AUC, so the ranking is even better
-   Barely above baseline on accuracy, and still catching well under half the Outstanding schools
-   **Not a quirk of one model.** This is what rare outcomes do, and you will meet it in your own data

## An uncomfortable question {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Progress 8 is by far the strongest predictor in both models. So what have we actually built?

::: incremental
-   Ofsted inspectors **read a school's Progress 8 score before they visit**
-   So we are not independently predicting a judgement - we are partly **recovering one of Ofsted's own inputs**
-   That is circularity, and it makes the model much less interesting than it first looked
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
And a second problem: inspection dates in this file run from **`r min(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`**, median `r median(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`. Some of these ratings were handed out a decade before the results we are using to "predict" them.

**Ask these questions of your own models.** They matter more than another decimal place of AUC.
:::

# Categories with an order {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## We threw information away {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   To fit a binary model, we collapsed four ratings into two
-   But Ofsted ratings have an obvious **order**: Inadequate < Requires improvement < Good < Outstanding
-   Treating them as a number (1, 2, 3, 4) is the mistake we warned about in week 1 - it assumes the gaps are equal
-   Treating them as unordered throws away real information

. . .

**Ordinal logistic regression** uses the order without assuming the spacing.

## The idea: cut points on a hidden scale {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 95%

ord <- polr(update(predictors, rating4 ~ .), data = train, Hess = TRUE)
cuts <- ord$zeta

x <- seq(-9, 7, length.out = 600)
tibble(x = x, y = dlogis(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = casa_teal, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cuts, colour = casa_red, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = c(-7.5, -4.3, -0.5, 4.5), y = 0.27,
           label = c("Inadequate", "Requires\nimprovement", "Good", "Outstanding"),
           size = 4.6, colour = casa_purple) +
  annotate("text", x = cuts, y = 0.02, label = sprintf("%.2f", cuts),
           size = 3.6, colour = casa_red, vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(x = "Latent 'school quality' scale", y = NULL,
       title = "One underlying scale, three estimated cut points") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
We imagine a single continuous scale we cannot observe. The predictors move a school along it, and the **cut points** decide which rating it comes out as. Three cut points for four categories - and the model estimates them from the data rather than assuming them.
:::

## Running it {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(MASS)
ord <- polr(update(predictors, rating4 ~ .), data = train, Hess = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
oc <- coef(summary(ord))
op <- 2 * pnorm(abs(oc[, 3]), lower.tail = FALSE)
tibble(
  Term  = rownames(oc),
  Value = round(oc[, 1], 3),
  `t`   = round(oc[, 3], 2),
  `p`   = ifelse(op < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(op, 3)))
) |> kable()
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
The last three rows are the cut points, not predictors. Everything above them reads like a logistic model: positive means *more likely to be rated higher*.
:::

## Did it work? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
pred_ord <- predict(ord, newdata = test)
acc_ord  <- mean(as.character(pred_ord) == as.character(test$rating4))
base_ord <- max(prop.table(table(test$rating4)))
within1  <- mean(abs(as.integer(pred_ord) - as.integer(test$rating4)) <= 1)
cm_ord   <- table(Actual = test$rating4, Predicted = pred_ord)
kable(cm_ord)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   Accuracy **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc_ord)`** against a baseline of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * base_ord)`
-   It **never once** correctly predicts Inadequate - `r cm_ord["Inadequate", "Inadequate"]` out of `r sum(cm_ord["Inadequate", ])`
-   But it is within one category **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * within1)`** of the time
:::

## So: can we predict Ofsted? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em"}
**Roughly, yes. Precisely, no. And the rare categories, not at all.**
:::

. . .

-   The model knows the difference between a likely-Outstanding school and a likely-struggling one
-   It cannot tell you which side of a single grade boundary a school will land
-   And it has essentially never seen enough Inadequate schools to learn what they look like

. . .

That is an honest, useful answer - and a far better one than a single accuracy figure would have given you.

# Categories without an order {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## When there is no natural ordering {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Ofsted ratings are ordered, so ordinal logistic is the right tool
-   But plenty of categorical outcomes are not: which region a school is in, which type of school a pupil moves to, which of five clusters a neighbourhood falls into
-   **Multinomial logistic regression** handles those - it fits a separate set of coefficients for every category against a reference

. . .

Let's fit it to Ofsted anyway, *deliberately ignoring the order*, to see what ignoring the order costs us.

## The comparison {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide
library(nnet)
multi <- multinom(update(predictors, factor(rating4, ordered = FALSE) ~ .),
                  data = train, trace = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
pred_multi <- predict(multi, newdata = test)
acc_multi  <- mean(as.character(pred_multi) == as.character(test$rating4))

tibble(
  Model = c("Ordinal (proportional odds)", "Multinomial"),
  `Parameters` = c(length(coef(ord)) + length(ord$zeta), length(as.vector(coef(multi)))),
  `Test accuracy` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * c(acc_ord, acc_multi)),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(ord), AIC(multi)))
) |> kable()
```

::: incremental
-   The multinomial buys about **`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (acc_multi - acc_ord))` of a percentage point** of accuracy
-   It spends **more than twice as many parameters** to get it
-   AIC mildly prefers it, which tells us the proportional-odds assumption is not perfectly met
:::

. . .

**Use the structure in your data when you have it.** The ordinal model gets almost the same performance from a third of the coefficients, and you can actually interpret it.

# Counting things {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## A different kind of outcome {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Let's change the question and move up a level.

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
*How many below-Good schools does each local authority have?*
:::

::: incremental
-   That is a **count**: 0, 1, 2, 3... never negative, never fractional
-   Most LAs have a few; some have none at all; a couple have a lot
-   A straight line will happily predict minus two struggling schools, which is not a thing
:::

## What counts look like {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 95%

la <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_schools = n(),
            n_below   = sum(below_good),
            mean_fsm  = mean(PTFSM6CLA1A, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_abs  = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5)

ggplot(la, aes(n_below)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = casa_teal, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = "Local authorities",
       title = sprintf("%d local authorities; mean %.2f, variance %.2f",
                       nrow(la), mean(la$n_below), var(la$n_below)))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
Discrete, non-negative, right-skewed, with a pile-up at the low end - **`r sum(la$n_below == 0)`** LAs have no below-Good schools at all. This is a Poisson-shaped problem, exactly as week 1 described.
:::

## But first - counts or rates? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Straight from week 1. Lancashire has `r la$n_below[la$LANAME == "Lancashire"]` below-Good schools and Bury has `r la$n_below[la$LANAME == "Bury"]`.

. . .

**Is Lancashire worse?** It has `r la$n_schools[la$LANAME == "Lancashire"]` secondary schools. Bury has `r la$n_schools[la$LANAME == "Bury"]`.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
We need to account for how many schools each LA had the *opportunity* to get wrong. In a count model that is called an **offset** - a term we force into the model with a coefficient fixed at 1:

$$\log(\text{expected count}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \dots + \log(\text{number of schools})$$

Move it to the other side and you are modelling a **rate**, not a count.
:::

## Running a Poisson model {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pois <- glm(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)),
            data = la, family = poisson)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
pc <- summary(pois)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term = c("(Intercept)", "Mean % disadvantaged", "Mean % absence"),
  Coefficient = round(pc[, 1], 4),
  `Rate ratio` = round(exp(pc[, 1]), 3),
  `p` = ifelse(pc[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(pc[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The link function here is $\log$, so exponentiating gives a **rate ratio**. And note the result: once average absence is in the model, **average disadvantage adds nothing detectable** - a confounding story of exactly the kind we met in week 6.
:::

## Checking the Poisson assumption {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The Poisson distribution assumes something quite strong: that the **variance equals the mean**. Real data often disagrees.

```{r}
#| echo: true
dispersion <- pois$deviance / pois$df.residual
dispersion
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A value near **1** means the assumption holds. Much above 1 means **overdispersion** - the data are more variable than Poisson allows, your standard errors are too small, and you will think results are significant when they are not.

Here we get **`r sprintf("%.2f", dispersion)`**, which is mild. So Poisson is adequate - but we should check rather than assume.
:::

## When it is not adequate {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
nb <- MASS::glm.nb(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)), data = la)

tibble(
  Model = c("Poisson", "Negative binomial"),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(pois), AIC(nb))),
  `SE on absence` = sprintf("%.4f", c(summary(pois)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2],
                                      summary(nb)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2]))
) |> kable()
```

-   The **negative binomial** is the Poisson's more forgiving cousin - it adds a parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean
-   This is exactly the distribution we met in week 1, and this is what it is for
-   Here the two models are essentially tied, so we keep the simpler one

. . .

**Fit the Poisson, check the dispersion, escalate only if you need to.**

## The fun bit: who beats their own odds? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| out-width: 95%

la <- la |>
  mutate(expected = fitted(pois),
         resid    = (n_below - expected) / sqrt(expected))

plot_la <- bind_rows(
  la |> slice_max(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "More than expected"),
  la |> slice_min(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "Fewer than expected")
)

plot_la |>
  pivot_longer(c(n_below, expected), names_to = "what", values_to = "val") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, n_below = "Observed", expected = "Model expects")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = val, y = fct_reorder(LANAME, resid), colour = what)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = LANAME), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~grp, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = casa_red, "Model expects" = casa_teal),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = NULL,
       title = "Where the model is wrong, and in which direction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Given their intake, some LAs have far **more** struggling schools than expected and some far **fewer**. The residuals of a count model are not a diagnostic afterthought here - they are the finding.
:::

# One more outcome type {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Proportions out of a known total {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Back down to school level, and to a file we have not touched yet: **what happens to pupils after Year 11?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest <- destinations |>
  inner_join(schools, by = "URN") |>
  filter(!is.na(COHORT), COHORT > 0, !is.na(OVERALL_DEST), !is.na(PTFSM6CLA1A)) |>
  mutate(not_sust = COHORT - OVERALL_DEST,
         prop     = OVERALL_DEST / COHORT) |>
  filter(not_sust >= 0)

tibble(
  ` ` = c("Schools", "Median cohort", "Median % sustaining a destination",
          "Schools at exactly 100%"),
  Value = c(comma(nrow(dest)), comma(median(dest$COHORT)),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(dest$prop)),
            sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", sum(dest$prop == 1), 100 * mean(dest$prop == 1)))
) |> kable()
```

-   Each school gives us "**x** of **n** pupils went on to education, employment or training"
-   That is not really a percentage - it is a **count out of a known total**, which is exactly what the binomial distribution describes

## Modelling it properly {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest_glm <- glm(cbind(OVERALL_DEST, not_sust) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A,
                data = dest, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
or10 <- exp(coef(dest_glm)["PTFSM6CLA1A"] * 10)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
Note the `cbind()` - we hand the model **successes and failures**, not a proportion, so it knows a school of 30 carries less weight than a school of 300.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
**Every 10 percentage points more disadvantage is associated with a `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - or10))` fall in the odds of a pupil sustaining a destination.**
:::

## Does it matter? Compare the predictions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

dest_ols <- lm(I(prop * 100) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A, data = dest)
gd <- tibble(PTFSM6CLA1A = seq(0, 100, length.out = 200))
gd$OLS <- predict(dest_ols, newdata = gd)
gd$GLM <- 100 * predict(dest_glm, newdata = gd, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dest, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, 100 * prop),
             alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, OLS, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, GLM, colour = "Binomial GLM"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Binomial GLM" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% disadvantaged pupils", y = "% sustaining a destination",
       title = "Same data, two models") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
They agree almost exactly through the middle and **diverge at the top end** - the schools policy cares about most. Here OLS is not obviously broken. It is quietly wrong at the edges, and **nothing in its output tells you so**.
:::

## And check the dispersion again {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
disp_dest <- dest_glm$deviance / dest_glm$df.residual
tibble(
  Model = c("LA below-Good counts (Poisson)", "Destinations (binomial)"),
  Dispersion = sprintf("%.2f", c(dispersion, disp_dest)),
  Verdict = c("Mild - Poisson is fine",
              "Overdispersed - use quasibinomial")
) |> kable()
```

. . .

-   **Two models, two different answers.** The check is not a formality you tick off
-   For the destinations model, switching to `family = quasibinomial` widens the standard errors by about 60% - the coefficients are unchanged, but our confidence in them was overstated

# Wrapping up {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## The family, in one slide {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| Outcome | `family =` | Link | Interpret coefficients as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | Units of y per unit of x |
| Yes / no | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| x out of n | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| Ordered categories | `MASS::polr()` | logit | Odds of being in a higher category |
| Unordered categories | `nnet::multinom()` | logit | Odds vs a reference category |
| Count | `poisson` | log | Rate ratios |
| Overdispersed count | `MASS::glm.nb()` | log | Rate ratios |

. . .

**One framework.** Change the family, change the link, and everything you learned about building and interpreting a linear model still applies.

## What carried over, and what didn't {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Still true**

-   The recipe: start simple, add complexity that earns its place
-   Confounding, mediation, interactions
-   Multicollinearity and VIF
-   Thinking hard about what belongs in the model
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Different now**

-   No R² - use AIC, deviance, or predictive performance
-   Coefficients need exponentiating before they mean anything
-   Residual plots look strange and need different diagnostics
-   Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced outcomes
:::
:::

## Where you can go next {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   **Generalised additive models (GAMs)** - when the relationship is smooth but not a straight line
-   **`glmer()`** - the intersection of this week and last week: a GLM with random effects, for grouped non-normal data
-   **Spatial and geographically weighted regression** - when the relationship itself varies over space
-   **Ridge and lasso** - when you have too many predictors and need the model to choose

. . .

You now have the two big extensions to OLS: last week we relaxed **independence**, this week we relaxed **normality**. Almost everything else is a combination of the two.

## Conclusions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   **Look at your outcome variable before you choose a model.** Week 1's data types were not an academic exercise - they determine what you are allowed to do
-   A GLM is not a new method, it is the same linear predictor with a different distribution and a link function bolted on
-   **Always compare against a baseline.** A model that beats "predict the majority every time" by half a percentage point has not learned much
-   Check your assumptions - dispersion for counts, and the threshold question for classification
-   And ask where your predictors came from. Our best one turned out to be something Ofsted had already read

## Today's Practical {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Building and interpreting your own logistic and Poisson models on the schools data
-   Practice at the bit that matters most: **interpreting odds ratios and rate ratios** in plain English
-   And deciding, for an outcome of your own choosing, which member of the family you actually need
